fields.title: Transactions: all or nothing
fields.keyTakeaway: A transaction boundary is the boundary of the "all or nothing" promise; beyond it, the product must design behavior for partial success.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: A user pays for an order. Money is deducted, but the order is not created. How does the system even allow such a state—and what does it do to prevent it?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: This is the most expensive category of bugs in a product because it cannot be fixed automatically. Data discrepancies regarding money generate support tickets, manual investigations, refunds, and ultimately a loss of trust that outlives the bug fix. A PM who does not understand where the transaction boundary lies cannot design failure behavior or support operations.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: A [[transaction|transaction]] is a group of changes applied entirely or not at all. Within it, the database provides four guarantees known as [[acid|ACID]]; two of them matter to the product.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **[[atomicity|Atomicity]].** Either all changes in the group execute, or none. If something goes wrong in the middle, the database performs a [[rollback|rollback]] and returns everything to its original state. The intermediate state "money deducted, order not created" never exists within a single transaction.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: **[[isolation|Isolation]].** Concurrent transactions do not see each other's intermediate states. This resolves [[race-condition|race conditions]]: two people take the last carton of milk simultaneously, both see "stock 1", both place an order. Without isolation, the stock becomes −1. With isolation, the second transaction waits for the first and sees 0.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: Isolation is implemented using [[lock|locks]], and they have a cost: waiting. Under heavy contention for the same data, this becomes a bottleneck. The extreme case is a [[deadlock|deadlock]], where two operations wait for each other forever; the database detects this and cancels one of them.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: The main limitation: **a transaction works within a single database.** As soon as an operation touches an external system—a payment provider, a partner's warehouse—atomicity is gone. The provider has already charged the money; you cannot roll them back with our transaction.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: For such cases, other mechanisms are used: [[idempotency|idempotency]] (repeated calls do not create a second charge) and [[compensating-transaction|compensating operations]] (not a rollback, but a reverse action—a refund). Both are visible to the user and therefore require product design: what to show in the intermediate state, how long to wait, when to call support.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: *Inside a single transaction:* create an order, create order items, decrease stock, record bonus deduction. All in one database, all either exist or don't.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: *Outside the transaction:* charging a card. The sequence is as follows—first, the transaction creates an order with the status "awaiting payment", then the provider is called, then the status is changed in a separate transaction. If the provider answered with success and we failed to record it—the order remains in "awaiting payment" while the money is charged.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: This state is inevitable, and the product must account for it. Solutions: an idempotency key so a retry doesn't charge twice; reconciliation with the provider every five minutes; a "payment processing" screen instead of an error; a rule for support. All these are product decisions, and they only appear if the PM knows that the transaction boundary passes right here.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: *Deliberately without guarantees:* product view counter. Losing a few during a failure is not scary, and a transaction for every view would cost more than it's worth.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: There are several isolation levels, and by default the database usually uses one that is not the strictest—some race conditions remain possible. This is a setting worth asking about if the product does anything financial. In distributed systems, a transaction across multiple services is impossible in principle, and patterns with intermediate states that are always visible to the user are used there.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: A transaction boundary is the boundary of the "all or nothing" promise; beyond it, the product must design behavior for partial success.
